platforms.title: Hip Pain Lying on Your Side: 4 Things That Actually Help
platforms.meta_description: Outer hip pain when lying on your side is usually a gluteal tendon problem, not bursitis. What the LEAP trial found on injections vs exercise, plus NHS tips.
platforms.body_html:
You roll onto your side to fall asleep and a deep ache starts over the bony point on the outside of your hip. You turn onto your back, then the other side, and by 3 a.m. you are awake again. Many people are told this is "trochanteric bursitis", get a steroid injection, feel better for a few weeks, and then watch the pain creep back. The modern name is greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS), and the thinking behind it has shifted: the main problem is usually the tendons, not the fluid sac.

Why the outside of your hip hurts at night

The greater trochanter is the knobbly top of the thigh bone you can feel on the side of your hip. Two buttock muscles, gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, attach there by tendons. They hold your pelvis level every time you stand on one leg, which you do with every step. A 2015 review by Grimaldi and Fearon in the Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy describes gluteal tendinopathy as the main local source of lateral hip pain, the condition previously labelled trochanteric bursitis, and notes it is especially common in women after the menopause.

Lying on the sore side presses your body weight straight through those tendons into the mattress, which is why night pain is so typical. The NHS hip pain page lists exactly this pattern, pain that can spread into the thigh and feel worse when moving or lying on your side, under bursitis, and says to see a GP if hip pain is affecting your sleep or has not improved after two weeks of treating it at home.

It is also far more common than most people assume. In the US Multicenter Osteoarthritis Study, Segal and colleagues (2007) examined 3,026 adults aged 50 to 79 and found GTPS on one side in 15.0% of women and on both sides in 8.5%, against 6.6% and 1.9% of men. The same study found that people with low back pain had 2.79 times the odds of GTPS, and knee osteoarthritis on the same side was linked to 3.47 times the odds. That is an association from a cross-sectional study, not proof of cause, but it explains why a good assessment looks at your back and knees too. Body mass index was not linked to GTPS in that analysis.

What happens when you treat the tendon, not just the pain

Education plus exercise beat a steroid injection over a year. The LEAP randomised trial (Mellor and colleagues, 2018) enrolled 204 people in Australia, mostly women with an average age of 54.8, who had lateral hip pain for more than three months and gluteal tendinopathy confirmed on MRI. One group had 14 physiotherapy sessions over eight weeks focused on load management and exercise, one had a single corticosteroid injection, and one was told to wait and see. In this trial, 77% of the exercise group, 58% of the injection group and 29% of the wait-and-see group reported success at eight weeks. At 52 weeks the figures were 78%, 57% and 52%, so the injection advantage had largely gone while the exercise group kept its gains.

Less pressure at night means better sleep. Avoid lying on the painful side. If you sleep on the other side, the top leg tends to drop forward across your body and pull the sore tendons tight; the NHS bursitis page suggests putting extra cushions around the affected joint while you sleep, and a pillow between the knees is the simplest way to do that. Avoid crossing your legs or standing with your weight hanging on one hip for long periods.

Getting out of low seats gets easier. The NHS hip pain advice says not to sit in low chairs because they put extra pressure on the hips, and to keep moving without overdoing it. For pain relief it suggests an ice pack wrapped in a towel for up to 20 minutes every two to three hours, alongside paracetamol or ibuprofen gel. Painkillers and ice calm things down; the strengthening is what changes the outlook.

You may be able to see a physiotherapist directly. According to the NHS, in many areas you can refer yourself to community musculoskeletal (MSK) services for physiotherapy without seeing a GP first. That matters here, because a structured, gradually progressed exercise programme is the part of treatment with the strongest trial support.

So why does it keep coming back?

Usually because the pain was quietened but the tendon was never loaded back up. An injection can buy a few good weeks, but if you go straight back to sleeping on that side, sitting in low sofas with crossed legs and doing nothing to strengthen the hip, the same tendons get squeezed again. GTPS is common, it is not a sign that your hip joint is wearing out, and most people improve with the right mix of reduced compression and steady exercise.

Tonight, put a firm pillow between your knees and sleep on your good side. If the pain is still disturbing your sleep after two weeks, book a GP appointment or use your local MSK self-referral. Get urgent help, through NHS 111 or your GP, if your hip is hot and swollen, the skin changes colour, or you feel unwell with a high temperature; call 999 if you cannot put weight on your leg after a fall. This article is general health information and does not replace advice from a clinician who has examined you.

Sources: NHS, "Hip pain in adults" and "Bursitis"; Grimaldi A, Fearon A, J Orthop Sports Phys Ther, 2015; Segal NA et al., Arch Phys Med Rehabil, 2007; Mellor R et al., Br J Sports Med, 2018 (LEAP trial).
